title: Developing and Evaluating a Large Language Model-Based Automated Feedback System Grounded in Evidence-Centered Design for Supporting Physics Problem Solving
extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether a large language model (LLM)-based automated feedback system can provide useful and accurate formative feedback for complex physics problem solving, rather than only for simpler conceptual tasks. The authors argue that physics problem solving requires multiple forms of knowledge and skill, making automated assessment and feedback difficult. They also examine a key risk of generative AI in education: students may trust incorrect feedback, especially when it is presented fluently and confidently.

The intervention was an online feedback system built around OpenAI’s GPT-4o and grounded in evidence-centered design (ECD). Students entered written solution approaches to physics problems, and the system generated short, analytic feedback tied to problem-specific evidentiary schemes covering conceptual, conditional, procedural, factual, mathematical, and metacognitive aspects of problem solving. The system used a two-step feedback cycle in which students received feedback on an initial attempt, revised their work, and then received a second round of feedback. The design aimed to constrain the LLM and reduce hallucinations by anchoring prompts in explicit model-based evidence structures.

The system was evaluated with participants in the German Physics Olympiad during the first stage of the competition. These were secondary school students in Germany who voluntarily used the web-based tool as a problem-solving training opportunity. The study collected 64 Likert-scale ratings of feedback usefulness and perceived factual correctness, along with 47 open-text explanations of those ratings. In addition, two human raters reviewed the generated feedback to determine its actual correctness.

The main findings were that students generally perceived the feedback as useful and highly accurate, and some appreciated its adaptivity. However, students also criticized limited adaptiveness when their valid alternative solution paths were not recognized. Most importantly, human review showed that about 20% of feedback instances contained minor to substantial factual or pedagogical errors, and students usually failed to detect these errors. The authors conclude that ECD-grounded LLM feedback is promising for supporting physics problem solving, but current systems still pose risks due to undetected inaccuracies and limited handling of alternative solution strategies. They recommend clearer warning mechanisms, feedback flagging, better support for multiple solution paths, and future integration of student models to improve adaptivity.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used here as the engine for an automated feedback system that generates natural-language formative feedback on student work.
identified_tools.use_case: GPT-4o was integrated via the OpenAI API into an evidence-centered-design-grounded automated feedback system for German Physics Olympiad participants, generating short feedback on students’ written physics problem-solving approaches across a two-step revise-and-feedback cycle.

findings.finding_summary: Students generally perceived the LLM-generated feedback as useful for supporting physics problem solving (M=3.6, SD=1.7 on a 5-point Likert scale). The paper reports N=64 usefulness ratings, with qualitative comments indicating some students found the feedback helpful and adaptive, while others criticized limited adaptiveness to alternative valid solution paths.
findings.measure: Student-rated perceived usefulness of feedback on a 5-point Likert scale

findings.finding_summary: Students rated the feedback as highly accurate (M=4.4, SD=1.0 on a 5-point Likert scale), but human review found the feedback was physically correct in 51 of 64 cases (≈80%) and contained 14 minor to substantial errors across 13 of 64 cases (≈20%). Errors included calculation mistakes, incorrect physical concepts or assumptions, inappropriate solution strategies, and misclassification of correct alternative approaches as incorrect; most errors went unnoticed by students.
findings.measure: Student-rated perceived correctness of feedback and expert-coded actual correctness of generated physics feedback

findings.finding_summary: There was no significant difference in perceived accuracy ratings between students who received correct feedback (N1=51, M1=4.4, SD1=1.0) and those who received incorrect feedback (N2=13, M2=4.3, SD2=0.9). A two-sided Mann–Whitney U test showed U=363, p=0.543, indicating students judged feedback as similarly accurate regardless of whether it was actually correct.
findings.measure: Difference in perceived accuracy ratings by actual correctness group

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical evaluation of a specific LLM-based feedback system with quantitative ratings and qualitative analysis, but it is not an RCT or strong quasi-experimental design focused on causal learning effects. The main outcomes are perceptions of usefulness/accuracy and expert error analysis.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows promising perceived usefulness and high perceived accuracy, but impact on actual learning or performance was not measured, and 20% of feedback instances contained errors. Overall educational impact is therefore unclear and mixed.
